title: KV Consistency Adapter & Checkpoint Protocol Notes
body:
Purpose and scope:

This doc captures design notes and experiment results for a small protocol we prototyped to keep KV cache state consistent across kernel switches and in-flight request replay. Goal: enable safe, low-latency kernel handoffs (Triton <-> TensorRT <-> custom CUDA kernels) without corrupting attention cache or introducing token-level regressions for streaming/long-context workloads.

Problem statement (concise):
- Serving runtime sometimes needs to switch kernels mid-session (preemption, fallback, different quantization path). The KV cache is large and split across shards and must be transferred or made visible to the new kernel with minimal latency.
- Naive copy-on-switch or blind invalidation causes extra latency (massive memcopy) or correctness issues (stale KV leading to hallucination/regression).
- We need an operationally simple protocol that: (a) ensures deterministic outputs after a handoff, (b) minimizes copy time for common case, (c) allows partial reuse of KV shards and streaming continuation.

Key ideas explored:
1) Versioned shadow-writes: keep a generation counter per KV shard. Writers append new entries to a write-ahead region while readers can continue reading from the previous generation until a commit flip is performed. This avoids a global stop-the-world copy.

2) Checkpoint + delta shipping: periodic lightweight checkpoints (compressed) plus deltas for recent tokens. On handoff, transfer only deltas newer than last checkpoint.

3) Ownership lease + CRDT-like merge: shard-level lease assigned to a kernel instance; when another kernel must take over, it requests lease transfer and performs a bounded merge (last-writer-wins for overlapping keys).

4) Replay-safe fence + request replay: rather than trying to move all KV bytes, the new kernel can replay the last N tokens (small) into its own KV after receiving a compact fence snapshot. This sacrifices some CPU on replay but simplifies consistency and is robust.

Tradeoffs we considered:
- Latency vs complexity: Shadow-writes reduce pause but require more complex memory allocator and per-shard generation counters. Checkpoint+delta simplifies memory usage but can add network I/O when deltas are large.
- Determinism vs opportunism: CRDT-style merges are opportunistic and can lead to subtle nondeterminism if kernels implement different numerics; replay enforces determinism (same model/ops) because it recomputes KV via the model's forward pass.
- Memory overhead: Keeping shadow regions or compressed checkpoints increases resident memory. For multi-tenant Dedicated nodes this is non-trivial.

Prototype we built (summary):
- Lightweight proof-of-concept inside runtime adapter shim: per-shard uint32 generation, small ring buffer for recent deltas (max 4MB per shard), and a fence message to signal safe switch.
- Fallback path for small sessions (<512 tokens): snapshot-and-copy (fast memcopy). For longer sessions: delta+replay hybrid: send delta header, then replay last 64 tokens into new kernel.

Microbenchmarks (representative):
- Hardware: 1x A100, RTX 6000 test node, Triton v2.17, TRT 8.6 custom build.
- Workloads: streaming chat with median session length 6k tokens (20% sessions <1k, 50% 1k-6k, 30% >6k).

Results (median of 50 runs):
- Snapshot-and-copy (full memcopy of 1.2GB KV): pause 320ms (bad tail latencies up to 900ms).
- Delta-only transfer (deltas ~12–64KB typical): pause 8–12ms network transfer + 3–6ms integration = 11ms median.
- Replay-last-64 method: delta header + replay cost ~ 14ms median. Deterministic output matched baseline in 100% of repeatable tests (fp16/amp path).
- Shadow-write approach (prototype allocator): warm switch 6–9ms, but peak resident mem +10% and increased GC-like complexity caused occasional 60ms hiccups under fragmentation.

Observations and interpretation:
- For long sessions, shipping full snapshot is unacceptable. Delta+replay gives the best tradeoff for deterministic outputs with modest latency cost.
- Shadow-write looks promising for highly concurrent streaming workloads where handoffs happen frequently and deltas are large, but the implementation complexity is high and we saw fragmentation issues in the prototype.
- Lease/CRDT pattern is attractive for multi-writer setups (multiple kernels updating shared KV, e.g., shard migration) but introduces nondeterminism unless we restrict to identical numeric kernels and add cross-checks.

Practical adapter protocol (recommended v0.1):
- Shard metadata: for each KV shard publish {shard_id, generation, last_token_index, checksum}.
- On planned handoff: current kernel appends a delta-footer describing last N tokens and issues a fence: "fence-ready" with generation G+1.
- New kernel requests minimal artifacts: 1) small shard metadata, 2) delta payloads only for shards with last_token_index > checkpoint_index. If delta size < 512KB and session tokens < 2k, use delta+replay-last-64.
- For unplanned/cold failover: new kernel resumes by replaying last 128 tokens (configurable) and marks session as "best-effort-recovered" in logs and metrics.
- Log metadata for end-to-end audit: handoff_id, original_kernel_id, new_kernel_id, generation_before, generation_after, replay_token_count, checksum_post_replay.

Integration checklist for Triton/TRT adapter teams:
- Add per-shard generation metadata to adapter API (RPC called kv_shard_info()).
- Expose a lightweight replay entrypoint in kernel adapter to accept token list and return commit ack.
- Instrument fragmentation and resident memory before enabling shadow-write.
- Add signal for "planned_handoff" so autoscaler can try to schedule low-traffic windows when possible.

Open questions and risks:
- Quantized kernels (8-bit/4-bit) produce different KV representations; replaying tokens on quantized kernel will not reproduce fp16 numerical values exactly. Need to define acceptable divergence thresholds and detection (per-response checksum delta).
- Cross-kernel numerical determinism: even fp16 paths can diverge due to different kernel math. We observed tiny floating drift but output tokens were stable for our test models; still needs broader testing across architectures (decoder-only vs encoder-decoder).
- Multi-tenant memory budget: snapshots/checkpoints may blow node budgets if many long sessions reside on same GPU. Consider per-session eviction policies and proactive checkpoint upload to external object store (fast NVMe) for long tails.

Next experiments suggested (short backlog):
- Wider model matrix: run delta+replay vs snapshot for MPT-30B, Llama2-13B, mix of fp16/int8 kernels.
- Fragmentation stress test: continuous shadow-write/evict cycle to trigger allocator edge cases.
- Quantized merge test: intentionally switch between fp16 and 4-bit kernels mid-session to quantify output drift and generate thresholds for auto-fallback to replay mode.

Operational notes & metrics to collect:
- Handoff latency p50/p95/p99, broken down by delta transfer, replay time, memcopy time.
- Number of restarts with "best-effort-recovered" vs clean handoffs.
- Post-handoff output divergence rate (binary check vs reference) and downstream user-facing errors.
- Memory overhead and fragmentation metrics when shadow-write is enabled.

Conclusion / recommendation:
- Roll out delta+replay-last-N (N=64 default) as the first-safe mechanism. It is simple, deterministic, and gives acceptable latencies for our observed token distributions.
- Keep snapshot-and-copy as emergency fallback (small sessions only).
- Pursue shadow-write as a second-phase optimization if handoffs become a dominant source of tail latency and if allocator issues can be mitigated.
- Continue measuring cross-kernel numeric drift and add conservative guardrails for quantized kernel switches.

Appendix: quick command snippets used in prototyping:
- Start handoff (controller): curl -X POST "http://adapter.local/kv/fence?handoff_id=hf-123" -d "{\"session\":\"s-42\",\"last_tokens\":64}"
- New kernel fetch (controller): curl "http://adapter.local/kv/fetch?handoff_id=hf-123"
- Replay call (kernel): curl -X POST "http://kernel.local/replay" -d "{\"tokens\": [\"tokenA\",\"tokenB\"], \"session\":\"s-42\"}"

Notes-to-self / TODOs:
- Add a small policy object in rollout config to tune replay token count per model.
- File a jitter bug for shadow-write allocator (ENG-1309).
- Share results with Triton adapter owners and schedule dev sync next Wed.

If you want, I can extract a short design-PR from this and add a minimal API sketch for the adapter RPCs (kv_shard_info, kv_fetch_delta, kv_commit_fence, replay_tokens).
